title: Post stitches
subtitle: How to work front post and back post stitches to create ribbing and raised texture
excerpt: Post stitches insert the hook around the post of the stitch below rather than into the top loops. They create raised vertical ridges and form the basis of crochet ribbing.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch variation in which the hook is inserted from front to back around the vertical post (body) of the stitch in the row below, rather than into the top loops.
A stitch variation in which the hook is inserted from back to front around the vertical post of the stitch in the row below, pushing the stitch behind the fabric.
The vertical body of a crochet stitch, as distinct from the top loops. Visible as a raised column on the fabric face.

content.text: Post stitches insert the hook around the
stitch post
of the row below rather than into the top loops. A
front post
stitch brings the raised column to the front; a
back post
stitch pushes it behind. Alternating the two across a row creates crochet ribbing. Patterns abbreviate these as FPtr (front post treble), BPtr, FPdc (front post double crochet), BPdc, and so on.
Working a front post treble
Yarn over as for a regular treble.
Insert the hook from front to back, then from back to front, going around the post of the indicated stitch in the row below. The hook goes around the post, not into the top loops.
Yarn over and draw up a loop. Continue the treble stitch normally: yarn over, draw through 2 loops; yarn over, draw through 2 loops.
Working a back post treble
Yarn over as for a regular treble.
Insert the hook from back to front, then from front to back, going around the post from behind.
Yarn over and draw up a loop. Complete the treble normally.
Making ribbing with post stitches

Work a foundation row of plain trebles. On the second row, alternate FPtr and BPtr across every stitch. On the third row, work FPtr over every FPtr from the previous row and BPtr over every BPtr. The raised columns on the FPtr stitches form the ribs; the recessed columns on the BPtr form the channels between them.
Common problems

items.symptom: The ribbing lies flat instead of having raised ridges
items.cause: The hook is being inserted into the top loops of the stitch rather than around the post.
items.fix: Check the hook path. For a front post stitch, the hook must go around the vertical body of the stitch from front to back and back to front again, bypassing the top loops entirely.

items.symptom: The rib fabric is pulling tighter than the plain fabric
items.cause: Post stitches naturally compact the fabric slightly compared to plain trebles.
items.fix: Go up half a hook size for rows that use post stitches. This is common in hat brims and cuff sections where post-stitch ribbing meets plain body stitches.

content.text: What to try next

Try a short ribbing swatch of 12 stitches (6 FPtr, 6 BPtr) over 6 rows. The raised and recessed columns should be visible within 2 rows and show clearly by row 4. Ribbing done this way is commonly used as hat brims, cuff edges, and waistbands.
